content:
Greetings everyone!

I am a recent Mathematics BSc and I'm currently learning Lean 4 along a fellow student and our Logic professor as an independent project. In the past few weeks I have worked my way through about half of Theorem Proving in Lean 4 and I would really like to start experimenting on formalizing something new on my own and eventually contributing to mathlib. My areas of interest include Set Theory, Ring and Group Theory, Algebra and Logic,

After researching on Missing Undergraduate Theorems, good first issues and other threads, I was thinking about experimenting with examples of Groups of small cardinality, until I found a paper (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.09769) which covers most of it probably. I am not sure if working with groups of order p^n has any value.

Another idea that I started researching is formalizing String Recursion Theorem based on Yiannis Moschovakis' approach (treating recursion on strings as a generalization of recursion on the natural numbers). I also experimented a little with the agent Aristotle and I have a rough proof skeleton (still a little hard to read, working through it). Before I dive too deep, I wanted to make sure I am actually doing something useful. I'm a bit concerned that this might either be duplicating existing tools (like List.rec) or just not a priority for the library right now.

Could someone advise if formalizing the specific theorem would be a welcome addition? If not, I would love to pivot and help with something that the community actually needs, so any suggestions and/or guidance would be greatly appreciated. Thanks in advance!

I often recommend not thinking about mathlib at the beginning. Instead, start your own project on your favorite topic (you probably also worry less about covering existing topic this way). When building your own project, you will discover some small missing lemma from Mathlib, and you can start contributing those. After enough small lemma contributed, your project might finally take a good shape and you can upstream it piece by piece

I don't think anyone has formalised the statement that if G is a group of order less than 60 then G is solvable.

I agree with Weiyi that your instinct shouldn't be "what can I get into mathlib" or "what can I do that's useful" -- that is quite a high bar for a beginner nowadays. You're better off starting with "what can I get compiling myself" or "how can I have fun with this".

If you want to learn, then I would recommend staying away from AI agents. If you just want to get something compiling then go ahead but note that nowadays anyone can get anything compiling with AI agents and this is the opposite of helpful, indeed it's money down the drain.

BTW if you link to arxiv abstract pages rather than pdf then it's more convenient for people on mobile.

Thank you all so much for this feedback! I was definitely falling into the trap of thinking "what does mathlib need" and stopped having fun with it. This was exactly the redirection I needed because I was getting obsessed with finding some gap. I will keep learning without the agents, start my own project on something I like and see where it goes from there!

@Kevin Buzzard Your suggestion to prove that groups of order <60 are solvable is a great idea that aligns really well with my interests. It seems like a fun and concrete project to build on my own, so I will start exploring it!

Thank you again for pointing me in the right direction (and for the tip about arxiv links!). I'll probably be back with more specific technical questions as I start proving things! :spock:
